summary: Segment Routing encodes an end-to-end path as a list of segments, and can run over MPLS or IPv6. This document describes the OSPFv3 extensions needed to support Segment Routing over the IPv6 data plane.

plainLanguage.summary:
Segment Routing over IPv6 steers a packet by giving it a list of 128-bit identifiers, each one telling a router what to do. For that to work, every router has to tell the others which identifiers it has and what they do.

RFC 9513 adds that to OSPFv3: a way to advertise the router's SRv6 features and limits, a new kind of link state advertisement carrying the locators, and sub-TLVs for the identifiers that belong to a particular neighbour.

questions: how does ospfv3 advertise srv6 sids
what is an srv6 end.x sid
subtitle: How OSPFv3 routers tell each other about their SRv6 locators, segment IDs and limits.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing over IPv6 steers packets with lists of 128-bit segment identifiers, but OSPFv3 had no way to advertise which SRv6 features, locators and segment identifiers each router has.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9513 adds an SRv6 Capabilities TLV, a new SRv6 Locator LSA with function code 42 that carries locators and End SIDs, and End.X SID sub-TLVs for links and neighbours.
tldr.outcome: OSPFv3 can now distribute everything SRv6 needs inside a network. It is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: End.X and LAN End.X sub-TLV types

today: RFC 9513 was published in December 2023 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the OSPFv3 counterpart of the IS-IS extensions in RFC 9352, and it points to RFC 9514 for learning these SIDs through BGP-LS.

sections.title: What the Extensions Add
sections.content:
The Segment Routing architecture of RFC 8402 lets a node steer a packet using an ordered list of instructions called segments, each identified by a Segment Identifier (SID). When Segment Routing runs on the IPv6 data plane it uses the Segment Routing Header of RFC 8754, and that instantiation is called SRv6.

This document specifies the OSPFv3 extensions needed to carry SRv6 capabilities as defined in RFC 8986. At a high level there are four pieces.

  • An SRv6 Capabilities TLV that advertises the SRv6 features and Segment Routing Header operations the router supports.
  • Sub-TLVs that advertise the various Maximum SID Depth values, which say how many segments a router can handle.
  • An SRv6 Locator TLV, carried in a new SRv6 Locator Link State Advertisement, which advertises the locator, a form of summary address for the SIDs the router has.
  • TLVs and sub-TLVs that advertise the SIDs on the router together with the endpoint behaviours they invoke.
sections.plainLanguage: SRv6 steers packets with a list of 128-bit identifiers. This RFC gives OSPFv3 four ways to pass that information around: what the router can do, how many segments it can handle, the address prefix its identifiers sit under, and the identifiers themselves with the action each one triggers.

sections.title: Capabilities and Maximum SID Depths
sections.content:
The SRv6 Capabilities TLV is an optional top-level TLV of the OSPFv3 Router Information LSA, and an SRv6-enabled router MUST advertise it. Its type is 20. It MUST be advertised only once in that LSA; when several are received, the receiver uses the first occurrence, and prefers the one in the area-scoped LSA over the link- or AS-scoped ones. Area-scoped flooding is required; link and AS scoped flooding are optional.

The TLV has a 16-bit flags field with one defined bit, the O-flag, which says the router can support the O-flag in the Segment Routing Header flags as specified in RFC 9259. All other flags are reserved. No sub-TLVs are defined in this document.

Algorithm support is advertised with the SR-Algorithm TLV of RFC 8665. The maximum SID depth values use the MSD types that RFC 9352 defines for IS-IS, because the registry is shared between the two protocols. There are four: Maximum Segments Left, which signals the largest Segments Left value the router will accept before applying the endpoint behaviour; Maximum End Pop, the largest number of SIDs to which it can apply the penultimate or ultimate segment pop behaviours; Maximum H.Encaps, the largest number of SIDs it can add in the headend encapsulation behaviour; and Maximum End D, the largest number of SIDs present in a header when it decapsulates.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router advertises what it can do and how many segments it can cope with. The capabilities TLV is a single record in the router information advertisement; the depth values come from a set of four types that OSPFv3 shares with IS-IS.

sections.title: SIDs, Locators and Reachability
sections.content:
An SRv6 SID is 128 bits and is split into a locator part, a function part and an argument part. A router is provisioned with algorithm-specific locators, and each locator is a covering prefix for all the SIDs on that router that use the matching algorithm.

Locators MUST be advertised in an SRv6 Locator TLV inside an SRv6 Locator LSA. The RFC introduces a separate LSA rather than reusing the Extended Prefix LSAs, so that base OSPFv3 prefix reachability and SRv6 locator reachability stay clearly distinct. Forwarding entries for the locators must be installed by receiving SRv6-capable routers when they support the algorithm in question, and the locators can use the same route types as ordinary OSPFv3 prefixes: intra-area, inter-area, external, and Not-So-Stubby Area.

SIDs received from other routers are not routable on their own and MUST NOT be installed in the forwarding plane. Reachability to a SID depends on the covering locator. The RFC warns that if some other prefix ends up as the longest prefix match for those SIDs, traffic will not be forwarded correctly, and gives two cases to avoid: another locator with a different algorithm, and another prefix advertised through the ordinary or extended prefix advertisements.

Locators for algorithms 0 and 1 should also be advertised with the extended LSA types so that routers without SRv6 support install a forwarding entry for the traffic. When a locator is advertised both ways, the prefix reachability advertisement wins, so that SRv6-capable and incapable routers do not end up with inconsistent forwarding entries.
sections.plainLanguage: A SID is 128 bits made of a locator, a function and an argument. The locator is an address prefix that covers all the SIDs on that router for one algorithm, and it is the locator, not the SID, that is installed as a route. If some other prefix is a better match for those SIDs, the traffic will go the wrong way.

sections.title: The SRv6 Locator LSA and Its TLV
sections.content:
The SRv6 Locator LSA has function code 42. The S1 and S2 bits carry the flooding scope, which the advertising router chooses to match the scope of the locator, and the U-bit is set so that the LSA is flooded even by routers that do not understand it. A router may advertise several such LSAs, distinguished by their Link State IDs, which the originating router chooses arbitrarily.

The TLVs inside the LSA use the format of RFC 3630: a type, a length, and a value, padded with zeros to a four-octet boundary, with the padding not counted in the length. Nested TLVs are also aligned on four octets.

The SRv6 Locator TLV has type 1. After the type and length come a route type, an algorithm, a locator length in bits from 1 to 128, the prefix options, a 4-octet metric and the locator itself as an IPv6 prefix of up to 16 octets. Six route types are defined: 1 Intra-Area, 2 Inter-Area, 3 AS External Type 1, 4 AS External Type 2, 5 NSSA External Type 1, and 6 NSSA External Type 2. Any other type must cause the TLV to be ignored. A metric of 0xFFFFFFFF means unreachable.

Four sub-TLVs from the extended LSA world may also appear: the IPv6-Forwarding-Address, Route-Tag, Prefix Source OSPF Router-ID and Prefix Source Router Address sub-TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: A router advertises its locators in a new kind of link state advertisement, whose function code is 42. Each locator record says whether the prefix is inside or outside the area, which algorithm it belongs to, how long the prefix is, a metric and the prefix itself. A metric of all ones means unreachable.

sections.title: Advertising End SIDs and End.X SIDs
sections.content:
The SRv6 End SID sub-TLV is a sub-TLV of the SRv6 Locator TLV. It advertises the SIDs belonging to the router together with the endpoint behaviours they invoke. The sub-TLV has type 1 and holds a flags octet, a reserved octet, a 2-octet endpoint behaviour code point and the 128-bit SID. An End SID inherits the algorithm of its parent locator and MUST be allocated from that locator; one that is not MUST be ignored. Every SRv6-enabled router SHOULD advertise at least one End SID for itself.

SIDs that belong to a particular neighbour, such as the End.X behaviour, which forwards to a specific neighbour on a specific link, are not advertised under the locator. They are carried by two optional sub-TLVs of the E-Router-Link TLV of RFC 8362. The SRv6 End.X SID sub-TLV has type 31 and is used for point-to-point and point-to-multipoint adjacencies and for the adjacency to the designated router on broadcast and NBMA links. The SRv6 LAN End.X SID sub-TLV has type 32 and is used on broadcast and NBMA links for the backup designated router and the other neighbours, and it carries the neighbour's OSPFv3 Router-ID so that one instance can be given per neighbour. Both carry the endpoint behaviour, the flags, the algorithm, a weight for load balancing and the 128-bit SID.

The flags are the backup flag, which says the SID points at a path eligible for protection; the set flag, which says the SID refers to a set of adjacencies; and the persistent flag, which says the SID value stays the same across a router restart or a link flap. Every End.X and LAN End.X SID must be covered by the subnet of a locator with the matching algorithm that the same router advertises, or it must be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: A router's own SIDs are listed under its locator, each with the action it triggers. SIDs that mean "forward to this neighbour on this link" are listed under the link instead, because they belong to one neighbour rather than to the router. Each of those records also carries a weight that lets traffic be spread over several links.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document adds extensions to OSPFv3 and so does not change the security considerations of OSPFv3 itself as documented in RFC 5340. RFC 7166 describes an alternative authentication mechanism for OSPFv3, and the RFC recommends using authentication when deploying OSPFv3.

Receiving a malformed TLV or sub-TLV SHOULD be counted and logged in a rate-limited way, so that a flood of malformed input does not fill the log while the problem can still be analysed.

The security considerations of Segment Routing in RFC 8402 apply, as do those of the SRv6 network programming model in RFC 8986. Advertising an incorrect maximum SID depth value can have negative consequences, and RFC 8476 has more on that. The RFC also points to the security concerns of the O-flag in RFC 9259 and of Flexible Algorithms in RFC 9350.
sections.plainLanguage: These extensions do not change how OSPFv3 is protected; use the usual OSPFv3 authentication. A router that receives a malformed record should note it, but rate-limit the logging so a flood of bad input cannot overwhelm the system.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content: IANA has made allocations in the OSPF and OSPFv3 registries and created new registries. The document lists them section by section: the OSPF Router Information TLVs, the OSPFv3 LSA function codes, the OSPFv3 prefix options, the flags of the SRv6 Capabilities TLV, the flags of the SRv6 End SID and adjacency SID sub-TLVs, the OSPFv3 extended-LSA sub-TLVs, and the TLVs and sub-TLVs of the SRv6 Locator LSA.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC registers the new codes it uses: the function code for the new kind of link state advertisement, the TLV and sub-TLV type numbers, and the flag bits each one carries.
